name: Security analysis of a custom hash-function construction
theory_paragraphs: A \term{cryptographic hash function} is a map $H : \{0,1\}^{*} \rightarrow \{0,1\}^{n}$ from arbitrary-length bitstrings to a fixed $n$-bit \term{digest} (a \q{fingerprint}). It must be \imp{deterministic and efficient to compute}, and it must satisfy up to three security requirements, each phrased as a computational-infeasibility statement (collisions always exist by the pigeonhole principle, so we can never prove their non-existence -- only that finding them is infeasible):\begin{tightitem}\item \term{One-wayness (preimage resistance)}: given a digest $h$, it is infeasible to find any $x$ with $H(x) = h$.\item \term{Weak collision resistance (second-preimage resistance)}: given an input $x$, it is infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\item \term{Strong collision resistance}: it is infeasible to find ANY pair $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\end{tightitem}Note the asymmetry: in the weak property the attacker is handed $x$ and cannot choose it; in the strong property the attacker chooses both. Hence \imp{strong collision resistance implies weak collision resistance} (a break of the weak game is automatically a break of the strong game), while one-wayness is a separate axis.

Exam constructions always split a candidate hash into two parts: a \term{secure primitive} $P$ (assumed secure, e.g. SHA256 or AES) and a \term{combiner} $C$ that mangles the input or output. Two shapes matter:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Combiner inside the primitive}: $H(x) = P(C(x))$, e.g. $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$ over 256-bit blocks. If $C$ is linear (xor, addition $\bmod\, 2^n$), its \term{cancellation} properties let you manufacture collisions at will, so the two collision properties typically FAIL. One-wayness usually still HOLDS by reduction.\item \term{Combiner outside the primitive}: $H(x) = P(x) \,\|\, C(x)$, e.g. appending $LSB_{128}(x)$. The primitive's output survives verbatim in the digest, so equality of $H$ forces equality of $P$: all three properties HOLD by reduction, but the construction is \imp{no stronger than the primitive part} (only $256$ of $384$ output bits do security work).\end{tightitem}

The two proof patterns to master:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Disproof by construction}: to break a property, EXHIBIT a concrete preimage or colliding pair and verify it. With a linear combiner this is algebra: for xor, duplicate blocks cancel ($b \oplus b = 0$) and permuted blocks give equal xor; for sums $\sum_i a_i x_i \bmod 2^n$, fix all blocks of $y$ but one and solve for the last (pick a block whose coefficient $a_j$ is odd so that $a_j^{-1} \bmod 2^n$ exists).\item \term{Proof by reduction}: to argue a property holds, assume an adversary $\mathcal{A}$ breaking it for $H$ and show $\mathcal{A}$ also breaks the corresponding property of $P$. E.g. if $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x) \,\|\, C(x)$ and $H(x) = H(y)$, then the SHA256 halves are equal, so $(x,y)$ collides for SHA256 -- contradiction with its assumed security.\end{tightitem}One more signal: if the exam remarks that $E_K$ and $D_K$ are \imp{mutual inverses}, the primitive is a block cipher with a KNOWN key -- you may apply $D_K$ freely when building attacks, so the usual \q{security of the primitive} reductions collapse.
theory_cheatsheet: One-way: given $h$, find $x$ with $H(x)=h$ must be infeasible (attacker chooses $x$ freely).
Weak coll.: given $x$, find $y \neq x$ with $H(x)=H(y)$ must be infeasible ($x$ is fixed by challenger).
Strong coll.: find ANY $x \neq y$ with $H(x)=H(y)$ must be infeasible (easiest attacker game).
Strong coll. res. $\Rightarrow$ weak coll. res.; to disprove weak, first break strong and check the trick also works with $x$ fixed.
Xor laws: $b \oplus b = 0$, $b \oplus 0 = b$, commutative/associative $\Rightarrow$ permuted or twice-duplicated blocks give equal xor.
Reduction template: $H(x)=H(y)$ forces $P(x)=P(y)$ or $P(C(x))=P(C(y))$ $\Rightarrow$ contradiction with security of $P$; a preimage of $H$ yields a preimage of $P$.
Linearity kills collisions, not one-wayness: inverting $H = P \circ C$ still requires inverting $P$ on some point.
Block cipher with known key: use $D_K$ freely -- the primitive gives no one-wayness against you.
identify_givens: A concrete hash $H$ built from a stated secure primitive (SHA256/SHA-2, sometimes AES with the remark that encrypt/decrypt are mutual inverses) plus a combiner: bitwise xor of input blocks, weighted sums $\bmod\, 2^n$, dropping/duplicating blocks, or concatenating input bits (e.g. $LSB_{128}(x)$) to the primitive's output. Often given as short pseudocode like `def hash(x): H = SHA256(x); H = H ++ LSB128(x); return H` or a formula $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$ over $n$ blocks of 256 bits.
identify_target: For EACH of the three requirements of a cryptographically secure hash function -- one-wayness (preimage resistance), weak collision resistance (second-preimage resistance), strong collision resistance -- (1) state the formal definition and (2) either disprove it by exhibiting an explicit preimage/collision or argue it holds, usually by a reduction showing an attack on $H$ implies an attack on the underlying primitive.
identify_keywords: disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met
strategy_name: Define all three properties, then break via combiner cancellation or prove by reduction to the primitive

algorithm.detail: Write out all three definitions BEFORE any analysis:\begin{tightitem}\item One-wayness: given $h$, infeasible to find $x$ with $H(x) = h$.\item Weak collision resistance: given $x$, infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\item Strong collision resistance: infeasible to find any $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.\end{tightitem}\imp{Strong collision resistance implies weak collision resistance} -- keep this in mind when ordering your verdicts.

Split $H$ into the secure primitive $P$ (SHA256/AES) and the combiner $C$, and classify the shape:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Combiner inside}: $H(x) = P(C(x))$ -- cancellation attacks on $C$ become possible.\item \term{Combiner outside}: $H(x) = P(x) \,\|\, C(x)$ -- $P$'s output appears verbatim in the digest; expect reductions, not breaks.\end{tightitem}

This is the attacker's easiest game (both inputs free). Exploit linearity/cancellation of $C$:\begin{tightitem}\item Xor combiner: permute the blocks, duplicate a block twice ($b \oplus b = 0$), or append a zero block. E.g. $H(x_1 \| x_2) = H(x_2 \| x_1)$.\item Weighted sum $\sum_i a_i x_i \bmod 2^n$: fix all blocks of $y$ except one, solve $a_j y_j \equiv C(x) - \sum_{i \neq j} a_i y_i \pmod{2^n}$ (choose $j$ with $a_j$ odd so the inverse exists).\end{tightitem}Exhibit the pair $(x, y)$ concretely and verify both hashes match.

Now $x$ is FIXED by the challenger. Ask: does the step-3 trick still work when one input is given?\begin{tightitem}\item Usually yes: e.g. xor two equal extra blocks into $x$, or re-solve the modular equation for one block of $y$ while keeping the same combiner value $C(x)$.\item If the strong-collision attack needed control of BOTH inputs, weak collision resistance may survive -- argue by reduction instead.\end{tightitem}

Check two escape hatches before claiming security:\begin{tightitem}\item Does the digest leak input bits directly (e.g. appended $LSB_{128}(x)$)? Leaked bits rarely break one-wayness alone, but say so explicitly.\item Is the primitive a block cipher with known key? Then apply $D_K$ to $h$ and build a preimage via the combiner.\end{tightitem}Otherwise give the reduction: any $x$ with $H(x)=h$ yields a preimage of $P$ on the point $C(x)$, so one-wayness of $P$ implies one-wayness of $H$.

algorithm.action: Argue the surviving properties and grade the strength
algorithm.detail: For each property that holds, state the reduction cleanly: an adversary breaking the property for $H$ produces a collision/preimage for $P$ (e.g. $H(x)=H(y)$ with the combiner outside forces $\mathrm{SHA256}(x)=\mathrm{SHA256}(y)$). Close with a strength note if applicable: \imp{a construction is never stronger than its primitive part} -- e.g. only 256 of 384 output bits come from SHA256, so the effective security is that of the 256-bit part.

variations.name: Xor combiner inside the primitive
variations.detail: E.g. $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_n)$ over 256-bit blocks. Strong collision resistance FAILS: any permutation of the blocks, or a block duplicated twice, gives the same xor and hence the same digest -- exhibit $H(x_1 \| x_2) = H(x_2 \| x_1)$. Weak collision resistance fails by the same trick applied to the fixed $x$. One-wayness HOLDS by reduction: a preimage of $H$ still requires inverting SHA256 on some input.

variations.name: Combiner outside via concatenation (all properties hold, but weakened)
variations.detail: E.g. $H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}(x) \,\|\, LSB_{128}(x)$. Trap: the appended plaintext bits LOOK like a leak, but they do not help invert the SHA256 half. All three properties HOLD by reduction -- a collision or preimage for $H$ forces one for SHA256 -- but the construction is strictly weaker than plain SHA256 since security rests only on the 256-bit part while the output is 384 bits. \imp{Do not claim this construction is broken}; the expected verdict is \q{met, but weaker}.

variations.name: Modular/weighted-sum combiner
variations.detail: Combiner $C(x) = \sum_i a_i x_i \bmod 2^n$ or a polynomial rolling hash. Collisions are linear algebra mod $2^n$: fix all blocks of $y$ but one and solve $a_j y_j \equiv C(x) - \sum_{i \neq j} a_i y_i \pmod{2^n}$. Traps: \begin{tightitem}\item If $a_j$ is even it has no inverse $\bmod\, 2^n$ -- pick a block with odd coefficient.\item Forgetting the modulus, or dividing instead of multiplying by the modular inverse.\end{tightitem}

variations.name: Encrypt/decrypt mutual-inverse remark
variations.detail: When the problem remarks that $E_K$ and $D_K$ are mutual inverses, it signals that you may APPLY $D_K$ when constructing preimages/collisions: the block cipher is NOT one-way for an attacker who knows $K$. Invert the cipher freely -- only the combiner constrains you -- and note that reductions to \q{security of the primitive} then fail.

original_problem:
A software vendor fingerprints download files as follows. The file $x$ is split into 256-bit blocks $x_1, \dots, x_n$ (the last block is zero-padded), interpreted as integers, and the fingerprint is computed as
\[ H(x) \;=\; \mathrm{SHA256}\Big( \big(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\big) \bmod 2^{256} \Big), \]
where SHA256 is the (assumed secure) SHA-2 hash with 256-bit output. For each of the three requirements of a cryptographically secure hash function (one-wayness, weak collision resistance, strong collision resistance): define the requirement, and either disprove the requirement or argue why the requirement is met.

original_steps.work: Definitions. \term{One-wayness}: given $h$ it is infeasible to find $x$ with $H(x) = h$. \term{Weak collision resistance}: given $x$ it is infeasible to find $y \neq x$ with $H(x) = H(y)$. \term{Strong collision resistance}: it is infeasible to find any $x \neq y$ with $H(x) = H(y)$.

Decompose: $H = P \circ C$ with primitive $P = \mathrm{SHA256}$ and combiner $C(x) = \big(\sum_i x_i\big) \bmod 2^{256}$ sitting INSIDE the primitive's input. The combiner is linear (a plain sum mod $2^{256}$), so collisions in $C$ -- and hence in $H$ -- can be manufactured algebraically. This predicts: collision properties broken, one-wayness possibly intact.

Strong collision resistance -- BROKEN. Take any two 256-bit values $a \neq b$, e.g. $a = 1$ and $b = 2$ (as 256-bit integers). Set $x = a \| b$ (two blocks) and $y = b \| a$. Then $C(x) = (a + b) \bmod 2^{256} = C(y)$ since addition is commutative, hence
\[ H(x) = \mathrm{SHA256}\big((1+2) \bmod 2^{256}\big) = \mathrm{SHA256}(3) = H(y), \]
an explicit collision with $x \neq y$. (Even simpler: $x = 5$ as a single block and $y = 2 \| 3$ both give $C = 5$.)

Weak collision resistance -- BROKEN. Now $x = x_1 \| \cdots \| x_n$ is fixed by the challenger. Compute $S = \big(\sum_i x_i\big) \bmod 2^{256}$. Build $y = y_1 \| y_2$ with $y_1$ arbitrary and $y_2 = (S - y_1) \bmod 2^{256}$. Then $C(y) = (y_1 + y_2) \bmod 2^{256} = S = C(x)$, so $H(y) = H(x)$, and $y \neq x$ except with negligible probability $2^{-256}$ (when $y$ happens to equal $x$ -- if so, pick another $y_1$). Concrete example: given $x = 7 \| 9$ (so $S = 16$), choose $y_1 = 4$, $y_2 = 12$; then $H(y) = \mathrm{SHA256}(16) = H(x)$.

One-wayness -- HOLDS, by reduction. Suppose an adversary, given $h$, finds $x$ with $H(x) = h$. Then by definition $\mathrm{SHA256}\big(C(x)\big) = h$, i.e. the adversary has produced a preimage of $h$ under SHA256, namely the 256-bit value $C(x)$. This contradicts the assumed one-wayness of SHA256. Note the attacker controls $C(x)$ only through the sum, but that does not matter: ANY preimage of $H$ is a preimage of SHA256.

Conclusion: strong and weak collision resistance FAIL (explicit collisions via the linear combiner); one-wayness HOLDS by reduction to SHA256. Security note: $H$ is unsuitable for fingerprinting downloads -- a malicious mirror can swap file blocks (or re-balance two blocks while preserving their sum) without changing the fingerprint, so integrity protection is lost even though inverting $H$ remains as hard as inverting SHA256.
